Project 1: Does the US Yield Curve Predict Recessions and Economic Growth?¶

1. Objective¶

The yield curve shows the interest rate (yield) the US government pays on bonds of different maturities. Normally long-term bonds pay more than short-term bonds. When the opposite happens, the curve is inverted, which has often been followed by a recession. (from Literature)

Using real macroeconomic and financial data from the Federal Reserve (FRED), this project asks:

  1. How does the 10-year minus 2-year yield spread behave over time, and how does it relate to the Fed's policy rate, inflation and unemployment?
  2. Is the spread different during recessions and expansions?
  3. How many months before each recession did the curve first invert (the "lead time")?
  4. Does today's spread help predict GDP growth over the following year? (tested with a regression)
  5. Which measure of the curve is the better recession warning: the 10-year minus 2-year spread, or the 10-year minus 3-month spread?

2. Data source¶

All data is downloaded programmatically from FRED (Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis) using the fredapi Python package. The series have different frequencies (daily, monthly, quarterly) and different start dates, so they're cleaned and aligned before any analysis.

3. Description of the data set and variables¶

Name used in this project FRED code Original frequency Starts Meaning
spread_10y_2y T10Y2Y Daily 1976 10-year minus 2-year Treasury yield, in percentage points. Negative = inverted curve
yield_10y DGS10 Daily 1962 Yield on 10-year US Treasury bonds (% per year)
yield_2y DGS2 Daily 1976 Yield on 2-year US Treasury bonds (% per year)
vix VIXCLS Daily 1990 CBOE Volatility Index, a measure of stock-market fear
fed_funds FEDFUNDS Monthly 1954 Federal funds rate, the Fed's policy interest rate (%)
unemployment UNRATE Monthly 1948 Unemployment rate (%)
cpi (-> inflation_yoy) CPIAUCSL Monthly 1947 Consumer price index (a price level). I convert it to the year-on-year inflation rate (%)
gdp_real (-> gdp_growth_yoy) GDPC1 Quarterly 1947 Real GDP level. I convert it to the year-on-year growth rate (%)
recession USREC Monthly 1854 1 if the US economy was in a recession that month (NBER dating), 0 otherwise
spread_10y_3m T10Y3M Daily 1982 10-year minus 3-month Treasury yield (used only in the comparison section)
yield_3m DGS3MO Daily 1982 Yield on 3-month US Treasury bills (used to check spread_10y_3m)

Variables I create myself: inverted, inverted_smooth, year, period (Expansion / Recession), and gdp_growth_next_year (GDP growth one year ahead, used in the regression).

4. Importing libraries and connecting to FRED¶

In [2]:
from fredapi import Fred
import pandas as pd              #To organise and manipulate data in tables
import numpy as np               #To perform mathematical calculations
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  #To create graphs.
import seaborn as sns            #built on top of Matplotlib and makes it easier to create statistical visualisations

fred = Fred(api_key='API_KEY')

5. Downloading the series from FRED¶

In [4]:
# daily series
spread_raw = fred.get_series("T10Y2Y")    # 10Y minus 2Y spread
y10_raw    = fred.get_series("DGS10")     # 10-year yield
y2_raw     = fred.get_series("DGS2")      # 2-year yield
vix_raw    = fred.get_series("VIXCLS")    # VIX volatility index

# monthly series
ff_raw     = fred.get_series("FEDFUNDS")  # Fed funds rate
unemp_raw  = fred.get_series("UNRATE")    # unemployment rate
cpi_raw    = fred.get_series("CPIAUCSL")  # consumer price index (level)
rec_raw    = fred.get_series("USREC")     # recession indicator

# quarterly series
gdp_raw    = fred.get_series("GDPC1")     # real GDP (level)

#these are raw data series. We will need to clean and process them before we can use them for analysis.

7. Data cleaning¶

Each step states the problem, the fix and the reason.

Step 1: Missing values inside the daily series¶

Problem: Treasury yields and the VIX are not published on public holidays, so the daily series contain gaps after they start.

Solution: I do not fill these gaps. Inventing a yield for a day with no trading would create false data. Hence, I average the daily data to monthly values in Step 2, and .mean() skips missing values, the gaps do no harm.

In [6]:
daily_series = {"spread": spread_raw, "yield_10y": y10_raw, "yield_2y": y2_raw, "vix": vix_raw}

for name, s in daily_series.items():
    s_after_start = s.loc[s.first_valid_index():]
    print(f"{name:10s} missing days after the series starts: {s_after_start.isna().sum():4d} out of {len(s_after_start)}")

yield_10y  missing days after the series starts:  721 out of 16916
yield_2y   missing days after the series starts:  553 out of 13156
vix        missing days after the series starts:  302 out of 9611

Step 2: Convert the daily series to monthly averages¶

Problem: the regression and several graphs need all variables on the same frequency. Monthly is the common denominator: it is the frequency of unemployment, inflation and the Fed funds rate.

Solution resample("MS").mean() groups the daily data by month and takes the average ("MS" = month-start dates, the same convention FRED uses for its monthly series).

In [7]:
daily_to_monthly = pd.DataFrame({
    "spread_10y_2y": spread_raw,
    "yield_10y": y10_raw,
    "yield_2y": y2_raw,
    "vix": vix_raw,
}).resample("MS").mean()

print("Monthly observations:", len(daily_to_monthly))
daily_to_monthly.tail()        #displays the last 5 rows of dataframe containing the monthly averages of daily series

Step 3: Transform price level and GDP level into growth rates¶

Problem: CPI is an index number (a price level) and GDP is a level. Neither is comparable over 50 years or meaningful in a correlation. The literature typically analyses inflation and GDP growth as rates of change rather than levels.

Solution: year-on-year percentage change. pct_change(12) compares each month with the same month a year earlier (12 months back). For quarterly GDP I use pct_change(4), i.e. 4 quarters back.

Missing months: by default pct_change silently fills a missing value with the previous one before computing. I set fill_method=None so that a month that is missing in the raw data stays missing, consistent with my rule of not inventing data.

Quarterly to monthly: I spread each quarterly growth value over the 3 months of its quarter. I first reindex to a full monthly calendar that extends 2 months past the last quarter (so the latest quarter also gets its 3 months), then forward fill with limit=2 so a value cannot spill into later quarters.

In [8]:
# fill_method=None: if a month is missing in the raw data (e.g. CPI), leave the result missing
# instead of silently filling it with the previous value
inflation_yoy = cpi_raw.pct_change(12, fill_method=None) * 100       # year-on-year inflation, %
gdp_growth_q = gdp_raw.pct_change(4, fill_method=None) * 100          # year-on-year GDP growth, % (quarterly)

# quarterly -> monthly: reindex to every month up to 2 months after the last quarter,
# then fill each quarter's value forward for at most 2 months
all_months = pd.date_range(gdp_growth_q.index[0], gdp_growth_q.index[-1] + pd.DateOffset(months=2), freq="MS")   #For example, quarterly GDP growth series ends in October. Extending the date range by two months allows it to include November and December as well.
gdp_growth_m = gdp_growth_q.reindex(all_months).ffill(limit=2)     #This changes the index to the monthly dates created in the previous step   #ffill means forward fill i.e. carry the last available value forward into subsequent missing observations.

#this operation does not calculate new monthly GDP growth. 
#It assigns the available quarterly growth figure to the next two monthly dates. 
#Therefore, the resulting series is a monthly representation of quarterly information, not genuinely observed monthly GDP growth.

print("Last values of inflation:")
print(inflation_yoy.dropna().tail(3))       #displays the three most recent non-missing inflation observations
print()
print("Last values of GDP growth (quarterly):")
print(gdp_growth_q.dropna().tail(3))        #displays the three most recent non-missing GDP growth observations

Step 4: Merge everything into one monthly DataFrame and fix the sample period¶

Problem: the series start and end at different dates.

Solution: pd.concat(axis=1) places the series side by side, matching rows by date. I then keep only the period in which the main variable (the spread) exists, from the first to the last date. Incomplete last month: the latest month is only partly over, so its monthly average uses just a few days and is not comparable with full months. The code drops it whenever more than 4 days of that month are still to come, i.e. when the month is clearly unfinished.

In [9]:
m = pd.concat([                                   #combines multiple pandas objects into a single dataset
    daily_to_monthly,
    ff_raw.rename("fed_funds"),                   #monthly fed funds rate
    unemp_raw.rename("unemployment"),             #monthly unemployment rate
    inflation_yoy.rename("inflation_yoy"),        #year-on-year inflation
    gdp_growth_m.rename("gdp_growth_yoy"),        #year-on-year GDP growth
    rec_raw.rename("recession"),                  #recession indicator
], axis=1)                                        #combining column-wise, placing the variables side by side and matching their dates.
m.index.name = "date"                             #names the index date

rows_before = len(m)                              #Counting rows before restricting the sample
start = m["spread_10y_2y"].first_valid_index()    #Finding the first valid index of the spread_10y_2y column to determine the start of the sample
end = m["spread_10y_2y"].last_valid_index()       #Finding the last valid index of the spread_10y_2y column to determine the end of the sample
m = m.loc[start:end]                              #Restricting the sample to the period where the spread_10y_2y column has valid data, from the first valid index to the last valid index.

print("Rows before restricting the sample:", rows_before)
print("Rows after:", len(m))
print("Sample period:", m.index.min().date(), "to", m.index.max().date())     #defining the sample period based on the minimum and maximum dates in the index of the dataframe m

# the last month is incomplete if the latest daily observation is not near the end of that month
last_day = spread_raw.last_valid_index()       #gives date of the latest non-missing daily spread observation
days_left_in_month = ((last_day + pd.offsets.MonthEnd(0)) - last_day).days   #gives how many days remain in that month.
print("Latest daily observation:", last_day.date(), "| days left in that month:", days_left_in_month)

if days_left_in_month > 4:
    dropped = m.index[-1].date()
    m = m.iloc[:-1]
    print("Dropped the incomplete last month:", dropped)    #if the last month is incomplete (more than 4 days left), drop it from the sample and print the date of the dropped month.

print("Final sample period:", m.index.min().date(), "to", m.index.max().date())

Step 5: Missing values after merging¶

Now I check which variables still have gaps, and decide for each one.

In [10]:
missing = pd.DataFrame({
    "missing_months": m.isna().sum(),
    "first_valid_date": m.apply(lambda col: col.first_valid_index().date()),
    "last_valid_date": m.apply(lambda col: col.last_valid_index().date()),
})
missing                #displays the number of missing months, first valid date, and last valid date for each column in the dataframe m

yield_2y 0 1976-06-01 2026-10-01

Decisions:

  • vix is missing before 1990 because the index did not exist. I keep all rows and do not drop the pre-1990 period, since that would throw away 14 years of data for the other variables. Analyses that use the VIX will use only the 1990+ months (pandas ignores missing values pair by pair in correlations).
  • The most recent months of inflation_yoy, unemployment, gdp_growth_yoy and recession may be missing because these series are published with a delay. I leave them missing and do not invent them.
  • recession is handled in Step 6.

Step 6: Completing the recession problem and fixing its type¶

Problem: the latest months have no recession value yet (the NBER announces dates late).

Solution: forward fill, which assumes the status has not changed since the last published month. Limitation: this is an assumption, and the most recent months are therefore unconfirmed. Then I convert the column from decimal (0.0 / 1.0) to integer, since it is a yes/no for whether recession took place or not.

In [11]:
m["recession"] = m["recession"].ffill()
print("Missing in recession after forward fill:", m["recession"].isna().sum())

m["recession"] = m["recession"].astype(int)

Missing in recession after forward fill: 0

Step 7: Checking duplicates, ordering and regular monthly spacing¶

Because a duplicated or missing month would distort every time-series graph, the lags and the lead-time calculation.

In [12]:
print("Duplicate dates:", m.index.duplicated().sum())
print("Dates in increasing order:", m.index.is_monotonic_increasing)

expected = pd.date_range(m.index[0], m.index[-1], freq="MS")
print("Every month present exactly once:", len(expected) == len(m) and (m.index == expected).all())

Duplicate dates: 0
Dates in increasing order: True
Every month present exactly once: True

Step 8: Checking that the variables agree with each other¶

by definition spread = 10-year yield - 2-year yield. If my columns do not satisfy this, one of them is wrong. Small differences can appear because FRED rounds to two decimals and because some days may be missing in one series but not in another.

In [13]:
gap = (m["yield_10y"] - m["yield_2y"] - m["spread_10y_2y"]).abs()
print("Largest mismatch (percentage points):", round(gap.max(), 3))      #finds the largest mismatch rounded to 3 decimal places between the calculated spread (yield_10y - yield_2y) and the reported spread (spread_10y_2y)
print("Months with mismatch above 0.05:", (gap > 0.05).sum())            #finds the number of months where the mismatch is above 0.05

Largest mismatch (percentage points): 0.001
Months with mismatch above 0.05: 0

Step 9: Checking for impossible values and outliers¶

since a negative yield or a huge jump could signal a data error. Extreme values that really happened (for example yields above 15% in the early 1980s, or the sharp rise in unemployment in spring 2020) are not errors and must stay, because they are exactly what we want to study.

In [14]:

print("Largest one-month change in the 10-year yield:", round(m["yield_10y"].diff().abs().max(), 2), "percentage")

Step 10: Saving cleaned data¶

In [15]:
m.to_csv("yield_curve_cleaned_monthly.csv")

print("Raw daily spread series:", len(spread_raw), "rows")   
print("Cleaned monthly data:   ", m.shape)        #m shape gives the number of rows and columns in the cleaned monthly data, indicating how many months of data are available and how many variables are included after processing.

Raw daily spread series: 13157 rows
Cleaned monthly data:    (605, 9)

Interpretation: The raw daily spread series had 13,149 observations, and the nine raw series differed in frequency (daily, monthly, quarterly) and start date (1854 to 1990). About 4% of days are missing in the daily series because of public holidays; I did not fill them because inventing yields would create false data, and the monthly averages ignore them. I converted the daily series to monthly averages, turned CPI and real GDP levels into year-on-year growth rates, merged everything into one monthly table, restricted the sample to the period in which the spread exists (June 1976 onward), dropped the incomplete latest month (October 2026) and forward-filled the recession flag. The VIX is missing for 163 months because it starts in 1990, one month each of unemployment and inflation is missing in the raw data, and the latest three months of GDP growth are not yet published; I left all of these missing instead of filling them. The checks found no duplicate dates, a complete monthly index, a largest mismatch of 0.001 percentage between the spread and the yield difference, and no impossible values. Extreme values, such as unemployment of 14.8% in April 2020, are real events and were kept. The final dataset has 604 monthly observations (June 1976 to September 2026) and 9 variables.

Interpretation: The cleaned dataset has 604 monthly observations from June 1976 to September 2026. The spread averages 0.84 percentage points with a median of 0.78, so its distribution is roughly symmetric, and its 25th percentile of 0.19 shows that the curve is normally upward sloping and inverted in fewer than a quarter of months. The minimum of −2.14 is the deepest inversion. The 10-year yield, 2-year yield, inflation and VIX have means above their medians, so they are skewed to the right because of extreme episodes such as the early 1980s and the market crises. The 2-year yield is more volatile than the 10-year yield (standard deviation 3.65 against 3.24). The mean of recession is 0.10, so about 10% of months (roughly 60 months) were recessions. Unemployment reaches 14.8% and GDP growth ranges from −7.4% to +12.6%, both reflecting the 2020 pandemic. The count row shows that the VIX is available for only 441 months because it begins in 1990, that unemployment and inflation each have one missing month, and that GDP growth has three, which I did not fill.

Creating helper variables¶

In [20]:
m["inverted"] = (m["spread_10y_2y"] < 0).astype(int)    # 1 if the monthly average spread is negative
m["year"] = m.index.year
m["period"] = m["recession"].map({0: "Expansion", 1: "Recession"})

# 3-month average below zero, used only to detect inversion EPISODES (avoids one-month flickers)
m["inverted_smooth"] = (m["spread_10y_2y"].rolling(3).mean() < 0).astype(int)

# quarterly dataset for the regression: average spread in each quarter,
# and GDP growth over the NEXT four quarters
q = pd.DataFrame({
    "spread": m["spread_10y_2y"].resample("QS").mean(),
    "gdp_growth": gdp_growth_q,
})
q["gdp_growth_next_year"] = q["gdp_growth"].shift(-4)
q = q.dropna()

print("Quarterly observations for regression:", len(q))
m[["spread_10y_2y", "inverted", "recession", "period"]].tail()

Graph 1: Line chart of the spread over time, with recessions shaded¶

What I plot: the monthly average 10Y-2Y spread for the whole period, a dashed line at zero, and grey bands for recession months.

Why: this is the central picture of the project. I want to see whether dips below zero are followed by recessions.

What I intend to learn: how often the curve inverted, how deep the inversions were, and whether the grey bands appear after the dips.

Why a line chart: the data is a time series, and a line chart is the natural way to show how one variable moves over time.

In [21]:
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(14, 6))
ax.plot(m.index, m["spread_10y_2y"], color="steelblue", linewidth=1.2, label="10Y - 2Y spread (monthly average)")
ax.axhline(0, color="black", linestyle="--", linewidth=1)
ax.fill_between(m.index, 0, 1, where=m["recession"] == 1, step="post",
                transform=ax.get_xaxis_transform(), color="grey", alpha=0.3, label="Recession")
ax.set_title("10-Year minus 2-Year Treasury Spread (US recessions shaded)")
ax.set_xlabel("Date")
ax.set_ylabel("Spread (percentage points)")
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Interpretation: The spread fell below zero before five of the six recessions in the sample: 1980, 1981–82, 1990–91, 2001 and 2007–09. The 2020 recession was not preceded by an inversion of the 10Y-2Y spread because it was caused by the COVID-19 shock, and the spread stayed positive throughout 2019. The deepest inversion, about −2.1, came around 1980, but the shallow inversion of 2006–07 was followed by the most severe recession, so the depth of an inversion does not indicate how severe the next recession will be. The 2022–24 inversion, the deepest since the early 1980s, has not been followed by a recession so far, which is an unresolved or possible false signal.

Graph 2: Line charts of the policy rate, short yield, inflation and unemployment¶

What I plot: two panels sharing the time axis. Top: the Fed funds rate and the 2-year yield. Bottom: inflation and the unemployment rate.

Why: an inversion happens when the short-term yield rises above the long-term yield. Short yields are driven by the Fed's policy rate, which the Fed raises to fight inflation. Plotting these variables shows where an inversion comes from.

What I intend to learn: whether the 2-year yield follows the Fed funds rate, and what inflation and unemployment were doing around the periods of inversion.

Why line charts: these are time series and I want to compare how several of them move together over the same dates.

In [22]:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(14, 9), sharex=True)

axes[0].plot(m.index, m["fed_funds"], label="Fed funds rate", color="darkblue", linewidth=1.2)
axes[0].plot(m.index, m["yield_2y"], label="2-year yield", color="firebrick", linewidth=1.2)
axes[0].set_ylabel("% per year")
axes[0].set_title("Policy rate and 2-year Treasury yield")
axes[0].legend()

axes[1].plot(m.index, m["inflation_yoy"], label="Inflation (CPI, year-on-year %)", color="darkorange", linewidth=1.2)
axes[1].plot(m.index, m["unemployment"], label="Unemployment rate (%)", color="darkgreen", linewidth=1.2)
axes[1].set_ylabel("%")
axes[1].set_title("Inflation and unemployment")
axes[1].set_xlabel("Date")
axes[1].legend()

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Interpretation: The 2-year yield follows the Fed funds rate very closely and often moves slightly ahead of it, so inversions come from tight monetary policy: when the Fed raises short rates to fight inflation, the 2-year yield rises above the 10-year yield. This is clearest in the early 1980s, when inflation reached about 14.6% and the policy rate about 19%, matching the deepest inversion in the sample. Unemployment peaks (for example about 10% in 2009–10 and 14.8% in April 2020) occur after the recessions begin, so unemployment is a lagging indicator, while the yield spread is a leading one. The 2022 inflation surge to about 9% and the following rate rises led to the most recent inversion.

Graph 3: Histogram of the spread, expansions vs recessions¶

What I plot: the distribution of monthly spread values, drawn separately for expansion months and recession months.

Why: a time-series chart does not show clearly how common each spread level is. A distribution does.

What I intend to learn: the typical spread level, and whether the two distributions are centred in different places.

Why a histogram: it shows the shape of a single numerical variable (centre, spread, skew). I use density instead of counts because there are far fewer recession months than expansion months.

In [23]:
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))
sns.histplot(data=m, x="spread_10y_2y", hue="period", bins=30,
             stat="density", common_norm=False, element="step", ax=ax)
ax.axvline(0, color="black", linestyle="--", linewidth=1)
ax.set_title("Distribution of the 10Y-2Y Spread")
ax.set_xlabel("Spread (percentage points)")
ax.set_ylabel("Density")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Interpretation: The spread distribution is centred slightly higher in recession months than in expansion months, with a thin left tail of strongly negative values, mostly from the early 1980s. The two distributions overlap heavily, so the level of the spread alone cannot identify a recession: the curve inverts ahead of a recession and has usually steepened again by the time the downturn is under way. The recession histogram is lumpy because it is based on only about 60 months from six recessions, and densities are used so that the two groups of different size can be compared.

Graph 4: Box plot of the spread by period¶

What I plot: the spread in expansion months versus recession months as two box plots.

Why: to compare the two groups with a few clear numbers: median, quartiles and outliers.

What I intend to learn: whether the median spread is lower in recessions, and how much the two groups overlap.

Why a box plot: it is designed for comparing a numerical variable across categories, and it highlights the median and outliers, which a histogram does not show as cleanly.

Hint for interpretation: think about timing. The curve tends to invert before a recession starts. What has usually happened to the curve by the time the recession is under way?

In [24]:
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 6))
sns.boxplot(data=m, x="period", y="spread_10y_2y", ax=ax)
ax.axhline(0, color="black", linestyle="--", linewidth=1)
ax.set_title("Spread: Expansion vs Recession")
ax.set_xlabel("")
ax.set_ylabel("Spread (percentage points)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Interpretation: The median spread is higher in recession months (about 0.97) than in expansion months (about 0.70), and the interquartile range of both groups lies above zero, so the level of the spread does not identify a recession. This is consistent with the curve being a leading indicator: it inverts before a recession begins, and by the time the downturn is under way the Fed has cut short-term rates and the curve has steepened again. The two low outliers in the recession group (about −1.4 and −2.1) come from the 1980 and 1981–82 recessions, when inflation and interest rates were exceptionally high. Because there are only about 60 recession months from six episodes, the difference should be seen as a pattern and not a firm result.

Regression: does today's spread predict GDP growth one year ahead?¶

Model: for each quarter t,

GDP growth over the next year = a + b x (average spread in quarter t) + error

Why: this tests the economics behind the yield curve. A low or negative spread signals tight monetary policy and pessimistic expectations, so we would expect b > 0 (a higher spread today goes with higher growth next year).

What to look at: the sign and size of b, its p-value (is it statistically different from zero?) and the R-squared (how much of the variation in future growth the spread explains).

Note on standard errors: GDP growth one year ahead overlaps in consecutive quarters, so the errors are correlated across time. I therefore use heteroskedasticity- and autocorrelation-consistent (HAC, "Newey-West") standard errors with 4 lags, which is the standard fix for this problem.

In [25]:
X = sm.add_constant(q["spread"])
model = sm.OLS(q["gdp_growth_next_year"], X).fit(cov_type="HAC", cov_kwds={"maxlags": 4})
print(model.summary())

Interpretation: The estimated slope is 0.37: one percentage higher spread is associated with about 0.37 percentage higher GDP growth over the next year, which has the sign predicted by theory. However, the effect is not statistically significant (p = 0.121, and the 95% confidence interval from −0.10 to 0.84 includes zero), and the spread explains only about 2.4% of the variation in future growth. The Durbin-Watson statistic of 0.51 shows strong autocorrelation, caused by the overlapping one-year growth windows, which is why heteroskedasticity- and autocorrelation-consistent standard errors were used. The residuals also have heavy tails (kurtosis 7.6), reflecting extreme episodes such as 2008 and 2020. The yield spread is therefore a weak predictor of next year’s growth in this sample, even though it has warned of most recessions. These results show association and not causation

Robustness check: excluding the pandemic quarters¶

Why: the 2020 pandemic produced the most extreme GDP growth values in the sample (a sharp fall and a sharp rebound), which had nothing to do with the yield curve. A few extreme points can drive a regression, so I re-estimate the model after removing the quarters whose "next-year growth" window falls in 2020-2021 (quarters from 2019 Q1 to 2020 Q4) and compare the two results.

In [26]:
q_ex = q.drop(q.loc["2019-01-01":"2020-10-01"].index)
model_ex = sm.OLS(q_ex["gdp_growth_next_year"], sm.add_constant(q_ex["spread"])).fit(
    cov_type="HAC", cov_kwds={"maxlags": 4})

comparison = pd.DataFrame({
    "All quarters": [model.params["spread"], model.bse["spread"], model.pvalues["spread"], model.rsquared, int(model.nobs)],
    "Excluding 2019Q1-2020Q4": [model_ex.params["spread"], model_ex.bse["spread"], model_ex.pvalues["spread"], model_ex.rsquared, int(model_ex.nobs)],
}, index=["slope on spread", "standard error", "p-value", "R-squared", "observations"]).round(3)
comparison
Out[26]:
All quarters Excluding 2019Q1-2020Q4
slope on spread 0.372 0.324
standard error 0.239 0.237
p-value 0.119 0.171
R-squared 0.024 0.024
observations 198.000 190.000

Interpretation: To check whether the pandemic drives the result, I re-estimated the regression after excluding the eight quarters whose following-year growth falls in 2020–2021. The slope changes only slightly (from 0.371 to 0.322), the standard error is almost identical (0.239 and 0.237), the p-value rises from 0.121 to 0.174 and the R-squared is unchanged at 0.024. The relationship therefore remains positive but statistically insignificant, and the weak explanatory power is not caused by the pandemic. The two extreme pandemic observations occurred at similar spread values with opposite signs and largely offset each other. Other extreme episodes, such as 2008–09, still contribute to the poor fit.

Checking the regression assumptions: are the residuals normal?¶

What I check: whether the regression residuals follow a normal distribution, using a histogram with a normal curve, a Q-Q plot, and the skewness, excess kurtosis and Jarque-Bera test, for the full sample and for the sample excluding the pandemic quarters.

Why: the usual p-values of OLS assume normally distributed errors. If the residuals are far from normal, the p-values are only approximate.

What I intend to learn: whether the assumption holds, where it fails (centre or tails), and whether the pandemic is responsible.

Why these tools: the histogram shows the overall shape, the Q-Q plot shows deviations in the tails, and the numerical measures put figures on them.

In [27]:
from scipy import stats

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 5))
resid = model.resid

sns.histplot(resid, bins=30, stat="density", ax=axes[0])
x = np.linspace(resid.min(), resid.max(), 200)
axes[0].plot(x, stats.norm.pdf(x, resid.mean(), resid.std()),
             color="red", label="Normal curve (same mean and std)")
axes[0].set_title("Regression residuals vs normal curve")
axes[0].set_xlabel("Residual (percentage points of GDP growth)")
axes[0].legend()

stats.probplot(resid, dist="norm", plot=axes[1])
axes[1].set_title("Q-Q plot of the residuals")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

pd.DataFrame({
    "All quarters": [stats.skew(model.resid), stats.kurtosis(model.resid), stats.jarque_bera(model.resid)[1]],
    "Excluding 2019Q1-2020Q4": [stats.skew(model_ex.resid), stats.kurtosis(model_ex.resid), stats.jarque_bera(model_ex.resid)[1]],
}, index=["skewness", "excess kurtosis", "Jarque-Bera p-value"]).round(4)
Out[27]:
All quarters Excluding 2019Q1-2020Q4
skewness -0.2916 -0.4608
excess kurtosis 4.6402 2.1932
Jarque-Bera p-value 0.0000 0.0000

The residuals of the regression are not normally distributed. The histogram has a sharper peak and heavier tails than the normal curve, and the Q-Q plot shows an S-shape with points departing from the line at both ends, consistent with an excess kurtosis well above zero and the very small Jarque-Bera p-value. The two most extreme residuals, about −10 and +10 percentage points, correspond to the 2020 pandemic collapse and the 2021 rebound. Because OLS does not require normal errors for the slope to be unbiased, and because heteroskedasticity- and autocorrelation-consistent standard errors with 197 observations give reasonable large-sample inference, the regression is still informative, but the p-values should be treated as approximate. The central conclusion, that the relationship between the spread and next-year growth is weak and statistically insignificant, does not depend on normality.

Interpretation: The residuals depart from normality. Excess kurtosis is 4.61 and the Jarque-Bera test strongly rejects normality (p < 0.0001). Excluding the pandemic quarters (2019 Q1 to 2020 Q4) reduces excess kurtosis to 2.17, so about half of the heavy-tail behaviour comes from 2020–21, but normality is still rejected, and skewness becomes more negative (−0.47), suggesting that large negative forecast errors from episodes such as 2008–09 and the early 1980s remain. Because OLS does not require normal errors for the slope to be unbiased, and because heteroskedasticity- and autocorrelation-consistent standard errors do not require normal errors, the main conclusion, a weak and statistically insignificant positive relationship, does not depend on this assumption. The p-values should nonetheless be treated as approximate, and a robust regression is estimated below as a further check.

Robust regression as a second check¶

Why: because the residuals are not normal and a few extreme quarters have a large influence, I re-estimate the model with a Huber robust regression, which gives less weight to extreme observations.

What I intend to learn: whether the slope changes much when outliers are down-weighted.

Note: this method does not correct for autocorrelation, so I compare the slope and do not rely on its p-value.

In [28]:
X = sm.add_constant(q["spread"])
rlm = sm.RLM(q["gdp_growth_next_year"], X, M=sm.robust.norms.HuberT()).fit()
print(rlm.summary())

If the model instance has been used for another fit with different fit parameters, then the fit options might not be the correct ones anymore .

Because the residuals are not normal, I re-estimated the model with a Huber robust regression, which reduces the influence of extreme observations. The slope is 0.296, close to the OLS estimate of 0.371, so the positive relationship does not depend on a few extreme quarters. The robust regression gives a p-value of 0.025, but its standard errors do not correct for the strong autocorrelation caused by overlapping one-year growth windows (Durbin-Watson = 0.51), so I do not treat this as evidence of statistical significance. The HAC-corrected OLS result (p = 0.121) remains my primary inference. Overall, all three estimates (0.37, 0.32 and 0.30) indicate a weak positive association, with the significance unresolved.

Graph 5: Scatter plot with fitted line, spread vs GDP growth one year later¶

What I plot: each quarter as one point, with the spread on the x-axis and the GDP growth of the following year on the y-axis, plus the regression line.

Why: this is the picture behind the regression. It shows whether the relationship is really a line or whether a few extreme points drive the result.

What I intend to learn: the direction and strength of the relationship, and whether there are outliers (for example, the 2020 pandemic quarters).

Why a scatter plot with a fitted line: it shows the relationship between two numerical variables, and the line summarises the average relationship.

In [29]:
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 6))
sns.regplot(data=q, x="spread", y="gdp_growth_next_year",
            scatter_kws={"alpha": 0.6, "s": 25}, line_kws={"color": "red"}, ax=ax)
ax.axhline(0, color="black", linestyle="--", linewidth=1)
ax.axvline(0, color="black", linestyle="--", linewidth=1)
ax.set_title("Spread today vs GDP growth over the next year")
ax.set_xlabel("Average 10Y-2Y spread in the quarter (percentage points)")
ax.set_ylabel("GDP growth over the following year (%)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Interpretation: The scatter plot shows a weak positive relationship between today's spread and GDP growth over the next year, with a fitted slope of about 0.37, consistent with the regression table. The points are widely dispersed around the line, so the spread has little power to predict growth in any single quarter, and even quarters with an inverted curve were usually followed by positive growth. The two most extreme observations, growth of about −7.4% and +12.5%, come from the 2020 pandemic collapse and the 2021 rebound at similar spread values, so they largely offset each other, which explains why excluding them did not change the slope much. The confidence band is widest at negative spreads because few observations exist there, and it understates the uncertainty because consecutive quarters overlap.

Graph 6: Correlation heatmap of the macro variables¶

What I plot: the correlation between the spread, the Fed funds rate, inflation, unemployment, GDP growth and the VIX, shown as a colour-coded matrix.

Why: the project uses several variables, and I want an overview of how they move together before reading individual relationships.

What I intend to learn: which pairs are strongly related, and the sign of each relationship (for example, how the spread relates to the Fed funds rate and to unemployment).

Why a heatmap: it displays many pairwise relationships in one compact picture, which separate scatter plots could not do. A correlation shows association only, not causation.

In [30]:
corr_vars = ["spread_10y_2y", "fed_funds", "inflation_yoy", "unemployment", "gdp_growth_yoy", "vix"]
corr = m[corr_vars].corr()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 6))
sns.heatmap(corr, annot=True, fmt=".2f", cmap="coolwarm", center=0, vmin=-1, vmax=1, ax=ax)
ax.set_title("Correlation between macro and financial variables")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Interpretation: The strongest relationship is between the Fed funds rate and inflation (+0.69), as the Fed raises rates when inflation is high. The spread is negatively correlated with the Fed funds rate (−0.63) and inflation (−0.50), because short-term yields follow the policy rate, so tight policy flattens or inverts the curve. The spread is positively correlated with unemployment (+0.45), which reflects timing and not causation: unemployment peaks after recessions begin, when the Fed has cut rates and the curve has steepened. The correlation between the spread and current GDP growth is only −0.12, consistent with the spread being a leading indicator that signals future rather than contemporaneous conditions. The VIX is weakly related to the spread (+0.10) and moderately negatively related to GDP growth (−0.39), but its correlations are based only on data since 1990 and are not directly comparable. These correlations describe association only and may be influenced by extreme episodes such as the early 1980s and 2020.

Lead-time analysis (for Graph 7)¶

For each recession I find (i) the month it started and (ii) the first month of an inversion that began within the 24 months before it. The gap between the two is the lead time.

How the code works:

  • m["recession"].shift(1) gives the previous month's value. A recession starts where this month is 1 and last month was 0.
  • The same trick on inverted_smooth (3-month average of the spread below zero) finds the first month of every inversion episode.
  • For each recession start, I look back 24 months and take the earliest inversion start in that window.
In [31]:
rec_start = m.index[(m["recession"] == 1) & (m["recession"].shift(1) == 0)]
inv_start = m.index[(m["inverted_smooth"] == 1) & (m["inverted_smooth"].shift(1) == 0)]

rows = []
for r in rec_start:
    window = inv_start[(inv_start < r) & (inv_start >= r - pd.DateOffset(months=24))]
    if len(window) > 0:
        first_inv = window[0]
        rows.append({"recession_start": r.date(),
                     "first_inversion": first_inv.date(),
                     "lead_months": round((r - first_inv).days / 30.44, 1)})
    else:
        rows.append({"recession_start": r.date(), "first_inversion": None, "lead_months": np.nan})

lead = pd.DataFrame(rows)
lead
Out[31]:
recession_start first_inversion lead_months
0 1980-02-01 1978-10-01 16.0
1 1981-08-01 1980-11-01 9.0
2 1990-08-01 1989-02-01 17.9
3 2001-04-01 2000-03-01 13.0
4 2008-01-01 2006-02-01 23.0
5 2020-03-01 None NaN
In [32]:
# inversion episodes that started during an EXPANSION and were NOT followed by a new recession
# within 24 months (possible false signals)
false_signals = []
for i in inv_start:
    follows = ((rec_start > i) & (rec_start <= i + pd.DateOffset(months=24))).any()
    started_in_expansion = m.loc[i, "recession"] == 0
    if started_in_expansion and not follows:
        false_signals.append(i.date())
false_signals
Out[32]:
[datetime.date(2022, 8, 1)]

Reading the table: a recession with no inversion in the window (NaN) is a missed recession (the signal failed to warn). An inversion that starts in an expansion and is not followed by a new recession within 24 months is counted as a false signal. I only count inversions that start during an expansion, because an inversion that begins while a recession is already under way (as in 1982) cannot be a warning of that recession. The most recent inversion may also simply not have had enough time to be followed by a recession yet, and the NBER announces recession dates late.

Graph 7: Bar chart of lead time before each recession¶

What I plot: for every recession that was preceded by an inversion, the number of months between the first inversion and the start of the recession.

Why: this turns the visual impression from Graph 1 into a number I can report.

What I intend to learn: the typical lead time, and how much it varies from one recession to another.

Why a bar chart: there is one value per recession, and the recessions are separate categories.

In [33]:
plot_lead = lead.dropna(subset=["lead_months"]).copy()
plot_lead["label"] = pd.to_datetime(plot_lead["recession_start"]).dt.year.astype(str)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5))
ax.bar(plot_lead["label"], plot_lead["lead_months"], color="teal")
ax.axhline(plot_lead["lead_months"].mean(), color="black", linestyle="--",
           label=f"Average = {plot_lead['lead_months'].mean():.1f} months")
ax.set_title("Months Between First Inversion and Recession Start")
ax.set_xlabel("Recession start year")
ax.set_ylabel("Lead time (months)")
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Interpretation: The yield curve inverted between 9 and 23 months before the five recessions it preceded, with an average lead time of 15.8 months. The wide range, with a standard deviation of about five months, shows that an inversion signals that a recession is likely within roughly one to two years but gives no reliable timing. The 2020 recession has no bar because the spread stayed positive throughout 2019, so the 10-year minus 2-year signal missed it. That recession was caused by the COVID-19 shock, which no yield-curve indicator could have anticipated. The 1980 and 1981 recessions are close together and were preceded by essentially one inversion episode, so the five observations represent about four independent episodes; treating them as one gives an average of about 17.5 months. The results are therefore indicative rather than precise, and they depend on the 24-month search window and the definition of an inversion.

Which measure of the yield curve is the better recession warning?¶

Motivation: there is more than one way to measure the slope of the curve. So far I used the 10-year minus 2-year spread. Many economists prefer the 10-year minus 3-month spread, because the 3-month yield follows the Fed's current policy rate very closely. The Federal Reserve Bank of New York's recession-probability model uses this version.

Question: judged on the same recessions, the same period and the same rules, which measure

  1. warned earlier (longer lead time),
  2. missed fewer recessions,
  3. gave fewer false signals, and
  4. did better at predicting GDP growth one year ahead?

Fair comparison: the 10Y-3M series only starts in 1982, so both measures are evaluated on the common sample from 1982 onwards. This excludes the 1980 and 1981 recessions, which leaves the recessions of 1990, 2001, 2008 and 2020. That is a very small number, so the results are suggestive, not conclusive.

Downloading and cleaning the two extra series¶

Same procedure as before: check the missing days, convert to monthly averages, align with the existing monthly data, and check consistency. Here the consistency check is 10-year yield - 3-month yield = spread_10y_3m.

In [34]:
t3m_raw = fred.get_series("T10Y3M")    # 10Y minus 3M spread
y3m_raw = fred.get_series("DGS3MO")    # 3-month yield

for name, s_ in {"spread_10y_3m": t3m_raw, "yield_3m": y3m_raw}.items():
    s_after_start = s_.loc[s_.first_valid_index():]
    print(f"{name:14s} starts {s_.first_valid_index().date()} | missing days after start: {s_after_start.isna().sum()} out of {len(s_after_start)}")

# daily -> monthly averages, aligned to the months already in the main DataFrame
new_monthly = pd.DataFrame({"spread_10y_3m": t3m_raw, "yield_3m": y3m_raw}).resample("MS").mean()
m["spread_10y_3m"] = new_monthly["spread_10y_3m"].reindex(m.index)
m["yield_3m"] = new_monthly["yield_3m"].reindex(m.index)

# consistency check
gap3 = (m["yield_10y"] - m["yield_3m"] - m["spread_10y_3m"]).abs()
print("Largest mismatch (percentage points):", round(gap3.max(), 3))

# common sample for a fair comparison
cmp_sample = m.loc["1982-01-01":].dropna(subset=["spread_10y_2y", "spread_10y_3m"]).copy()
print("Common sample:", cmp_sample.index.min().date(), "to", cmp_sample.index.max().date(), "|", len(cmp_sample), "months")

spread_10y_3m  starts 1982-01-04 | missing days after start: 485 out of 11698
yield_3m       starts 1981-09-01 | missing days after start: 493 out of 11786
Largest mismatch (percentage points): 0.005
Common sample: 1982-01-01 to 2026-10-01 | 538 months

Evaluating each measure with identical rules¶

I wrap the lead-time and false-signal logic from before in a function, so exactly the same rules are applied to both measures (3-month average below zero marks an inversion; 24-month look-back window; a false signal is an inversion that starts in an expansion and is not followed by a new recession within 24 months).

In [35]:
def evaluate_signal(spread, recession, window=24):
    flag = (spread.rolling(3).mean() < 0).astype(int)
    inv_start = flag.index[(flag == 1) & (flag.shift(1) == 0)]
    rec_start = recession.index[(recession == 1) & (recession.shift(1) == 0)]

    rows = []
    for r in rec_start:
        w = inv_start[(inv_start < r) & (inv_start >= r - pd.DateOffset(months=window))]
        if len(w) > 0:
            rows.append({"recession_start": r.date(), "lead_months": round((r - w[0]).days / 30.44, 1)})
        else:
            rows.append({"recession_start": r.date(), "lead_months": np.nan})

    false_sig = [i.date() for i in inv_start
                 if recession.loc[i] == 0
                 and not ((rec_start > i) & (rec_start <= i + pd.DateOffset(months=window))).any()]
    return pd.DataFrame(rows), false_sig

lead_2y, false_2y = evaluate_signal(cmp_sample["spread_10y_2y"], cmp_sample["recession"])
lead_3m, false_3m = evaluate_signal(cmp_sample["spread_10y_3m"], cmp_sample["recession"])

lead_cmp = lead_2y.rename(columns={"lead_months": "lead_10y_2y"})
lead_cmp["lead_10y_3m"] = lead_3m["lead_months"]
lead_cmp

def summarise(lead, false_sig, spread):
    return {
        "Recessions in sample": len(lead),
        "Preceded by an inversion": int(lead["lead_months"].notna().sum()),
        "Average lead time (months)": round(lead["lead_months"].mean(), 1),
        "Shortest lead (months)": lead["lead_months"].min(),
        "Longest lead (months)": lead["lead_months"].max(),
        "False signals": len(false_sig),
        "Deepest inversion (pp)": round(spread.min(), 2),
        "Share of months inverted (%)": round((spread < 0).mean() * 100, 1),
    }

summary = pd.DataFrame({
    "10Y-2Y": summarise(lead_2y, false_2y, cmp_sample["spread_10y_2y"]),
    "10Y-3M": summarise(lead_3m, false_3m, cmp_sample["spread_10y_3m"]),
})
print("False-signal start dates, 10Y-2Y:", false_2y)
print("False-signal start dates, 10Y-3M:", false_3m)
summary

Interpretation of the summary table: The 10Y-3M spread preceded all four recessions in the common sample (1990, 2001, 2008 and 2020), while the 10Y-2Y spread preceded three and missed 2020. However, the 2-year measure gave earlier warnings: on the three recessions that both measures caught, its lead times were 17.9, 13.0 and 23.0 months (average 18.0) against 13.0, 8.0 and 17.0 months (average 12.7) for the 3-month measure, a difference of about five to six months each time. The 3-month average of 11.8 in the table includes 2020, so it is not directly comparable with 18.0. The 3-month spread inverted more deeply (−1.73 against −0.93 percentage points) but was not inverted more often (10.8% of months against 12.1%). The false-signal counts (1 against 3) overstate the difference: the August and November 2022 inversions are the same episode, which has not been followed by a recession so far, and the two 2025 episodes of the 10Y-3M cannot be judged yet because 24 months have not passed. Neither measure is clearly better; there is a trade-off between earlier warnings and fewer missed recessions.

Predicting GDP growth: the same regression for both measures¶

I repeat the regression from before, GDP growth over the next year = a + b x spread, once for each measure, on exactly the same quarters, with the same HAC standard errors, so the R-squared values are directly comparable.

In [37]:
q2 = pd.DataFrame({
    "spread_10y_2y": m["spread_10y_2y"].resample("QS").mean(),
    "spread_10y_3m": m["spread_10y_3m"].resample("QS").mean(),
    "gdp_growth": gdp_growth_q,
})
q2["gdp_growth_next_year"] = q2["gdp_growth"].shift(-4)
q2 = q2.dropna()

reg_rows = {}
for col in ["spread_10y_2y", "spread_10y_3m"]:
    res = sm.OLS(q2["gdp_growth_next_year"], sm.add_constant(q2[col])).fit(
        cov_type="HAC", cov_kwds={"maxlags": 4})
    reg_rows[col] = {"slope": res.params[col], "std error": res.bse[col],
                     "p-value": res.pvalues[col], "R-squared": res.rsquared,
                     "observations": int(res.nobs)}

pd.DataFrame(reg_rows).round(3)

Interpretation: Estimated on the same 174 quarters since 1982, the 10-year minus 3-month spread has a positive slope of 0.285 (p = 0.088, R-squared = 0.029), while the 10-year minus 2-year spread has a slope close to zero (0.043, p = 0.840, R-squared = 0.000). The 3-month measure is therefore the better predictor of next-year growth, although its relationship is only significant at the 10% level and explains less than 3% of the variation. The result also shows that the 10Y-2Y slope depends on the sample period: it was 0.371 in the full sample from 1976 but is almost zero from 1982, so the positive relationship in the full sample comes mainly from the early period.

Graph 8: Line chart of the two spreads together¶

What I plot: the 10Y-2Y and 10Y-3M spreads on the same axes from 1982, with a dashed zero line and recessions shaded.

Why: the summary table gives numbers, but I want to see when each measure turned negative relative to each recession.

What I intend to learn: which measure inverts first, which inverts more deeply, and whether either one inverts before the 2020 recession.

Why a line chart: both are time series on the same scale, so overlaying them makes the differences in timing visible.

In [38]:
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(14, 6))
ax.plot(cmp_sample.index, cmp_sample["spread_10y_2y"], color="steelblue", linewidth=1.3, label="10Y - 2Y")
ax.plot(cmp_sample.index, cmp_sample["spread_10y_3m"], color="darkorange", linewidth=1.3, label="10Y - 3M")
ax.axhline(0, color="black", linestyle="--", linewidth=1)
ax.fill_between(cmp_sample.index, 0, 1, where=cmp_sample["recession"] == 1, step="post",
                transform=ax.get_xaxis_transform(), color="grey", alpha=0.3, label="Recession")
ax.set_title("Two Measures of the Yield Curve (monthly averages, US recessions shaded)")
ax.set_xlabel("Date")
ax.set_ylabel("Spread (percentage points)")
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Interpretation: Both measures follow the same broad pattern, falling below zero before recessions and rising sharply during and after them, but the 10-year minus 3-month spread has a wider range and inverts more deeply in most episodes: about −0.7 before the 2001 recession, −0.5 before 2008 and −1.7 in 2022–24, against about −0.4, −0.15 and −0.9 for the 10-year minus 2-year spread. The most important difference is 2019: the 10Y-3M spread fell below zero, while the 10Y-2Y spread stayed at about zero, so only the 3-month measure gave a warning before the 2020 recession. The 3-month yield is closely tied to the current policy rate, whereas the 2-year yield also reflects expected future policy, which may explain why the two measures behave differently. The comparison rests on only four recessions, so these differences are suggestive and not conclusive.

Graph 9: Grouped bar chart of lead times for both measures¶

What I plot: for each recession in the common sample, two bars: the lead time of the 10Y-2Y signal and of the 10Y-3M signal. A recession with no warning is labelled "missed".

Why: it compares the two measures recession by recession on the same scale.

What I intend to learn: which measure gave the earlier and more reliable warning, and whether one of them missed a recession the other caught.

Why a grouped bar chart: there is one value per recession and per measure, and bars placed side by side make direct comparison easy.

In [39]:

Interpretation: Over the three recessions that both measures anticipated (1990, 2001 and 2008), the 10-year minus 2-year spread inverted earlier than the 10-year minus 3-month spread by about 5 to 6 months each time, giving average lead times of roughly 18 and 13 months respectively. However, the 10Y-2Y measure missed the 2020 recession, while the 10Y-3M measure gave a warning about 9 months ahead. There is therefore a trade-off in this sample: the 2-year measure warns earlier but missed one of four recessions, while the 3-month measure warns later but missed none. Because the 2020 recession was caused by the COVID-19 shock, which no yield-curve measure could have predicted, the 3-month measure’s apparent success should be seen as a coincidence of timing and not as evidence of foresight. With only four recessions, these differences are suggestive rather than conclusive.

What I conclude from the comparison: On the common sample from 1982, both measures were evaluated on the same four recessions with identical rules. The 10-year minus 3-month spread preceded all four, while the 10-year minus 2-year spread preceded three and missed 2020. However, the 2-year measure gave earlier warnings: on the three recessions both caught, its average lead was about 18 months against about 12.7 months for the 3-month measure. The 3-month spread inverted more deeply (−1.73 against −0.93 percentage points) and also predicted next-year GDP growth better (slope 0.285 against 0.043, R-squared 0.029 against 0.000), although its slope is significant only at the 10% level. The false-signal counts (3 against 1) overstate the difference, because the 2022 inversion is a false signal for both measures so far and the two 2025 episodes cannot be judged yet. There is therefore a trade-off: the 2-year measure warns earlier, while the 3-month measure missed no recession and was the better growth predictor. Because the 2020 recession was caused by the COVID-19 shock, the 3-month measure's success in that case should be seen as a coincidence of timing, and with only four recessions the comparison is suggestive rather than conclusive.

Limitations of this project¶

  • Small sample: there are only about six recessions in the data, and 1980 and 1981 are really one “double-dip” period, so there are roughly five independent episodes, four of which were preceded by an inversion. Averages such as the mean lead time are only indicative.
  • Arbitrary window: I search for an inversion in the 24 months before a recession. The 2008 lead time (23 months) is very close to this limit, and a different window could change the results.
  • Missed recession: 2020 had no preceding inversion. That recession was triggered by an outside shock (COVID-19), which no yield-curve signal could anticipate.
  • Possible false signal: the inversion that began in 2022 has not been followed by a recession so far. The NBER announces recession dates with a long delay, and the recent months of the recession flag are carried forward and are unconfirmed.
  • Weak statistical prediction of growth: the regression slope is positive (about 0.37) but not statistically significant (p about 0.12), and the spread explains only about 2% of next-year GDP growth (R-squared about 0.02). The yield curve is therefore a poor point predictor of growth in this sample, even if it has warned of recessions.
  • Overlapping observations: next-year growth overlaps across consecutive quarters, so the quarterly observations are not independent. HAC standard errors correct for this but the effective sample is smaller than 197.
  • Association, not causation: correlations and regressions show that variables move together, not that one causes the other. For example, the spread is positively correlated with unemployment because of timing (the curve steepens after the Fed cuts rates), not because a wider spread raises unemployment.
  • Comparison of the two measures: the 10Y-3M series starts in 1982, so the comparison covers only four recessions (1990, 2001, 2008, 2020). Differences between the two measures are suggestive, not conclusive.
  • Data limits: the data starts in 1976, so the 1970s recessions are not covered. Monthly averages hide daily movements, and the VIX only exists from 1990.
  • Non-normal residuals: the residuals have heavy tails (excess kurtosis about 4.6, Jarque-Bera p < 0.0001), partly because of the 2020-21 pandemic quarters. The slope is similar across OLS, the sample excluding the pandemic and the robust regression, but the reported p-values should be treated as approximate.
  • Sample dependence: the 10Y-2Y regression slope is 0.37 over 1976-2026 but only 0.04 over 1982-2026, so the full-sample relationship is driven by the early period. The 10Y-3M spread performs somewhat better over 1982-2026 (slope 0.29, p = 0.088).
  • False-signal counts are not fully comparable: the 2022 inversion counts as a false signal for both measures so far, and the two 2025 episodes for the 10Y-3M measure cannot be judged yet because 24 months have not passed.

Overall conclusion¶

This project asked whether the US yield curve, measured by the 10-year minus 2-year Treasury spread, warns of recessions and slower growth.

Recessions: The spread behaved as a leading indicator. It fell below zero before five of the six recessions in the sample (1980, 1981–82, 1990–91, 2001 and 2007–09), by 9 to 23 months, with an average lead time of 15.8 months. The level of the spread does not identify a recession: the median spread was higher in recession months than in expansion months, because the curve inverts ahead of a downturn and steepens again once the Fed cuts rates. Inversions come from tight monetary policy: the 2-year yield follows the Fed funds rate closely, and the deepest inversion (about −2.1) coincided with inflation near 14.6% and a policy rate near 19% in the early 1980s.

Growth: As a predictor of growth the spread was weak. The regression slope was positive (0.37) but not statistically significant (p = 0.121), and the spread explained only 2.4% of next-year GDP growth. The slope was similar without the pandemic quarters (0.32) and with a robust regression (0.30), but the residuals are not normal, so the p-values are approximate, and the slope depends on the sample period (about 0.04 from 1982).

Comparison of measures: The 10Y-3M spread caught all four recessions since 1982 and predicted growth better, while the 10Y-2Y spread warned about five to six months earlier but missed 2020.

The 2020 recession was caused by the COVID-19 shock and was missed by the 10Y-2Y measure; the 2022–24 inversion has not been followed by a recession so far; the sample contains only about six recessions, with 1980 and 1981 forming a double dip; observations in the regression overlap; and the results show association, not causation.

To conclude I want to say that the yield curve is a useful but imperfect warning signal. It has preceded most recessions by roughly one to two years, but the timing varies widely, it is a poor point predictor of growth, and its performance depends on which measure and which period are used.
